options: A mechanism built into databases like SQL Server and PostgreSQL that records every row-level insert, update, and delete as it happens
A KQL function for computing time series
A Power BI report refresh setting
A Fabric Capacity billing feature
questions.explain: Fabric's Eventstream can use CDC directly as a source type, turning a database's change log into a live event stream.

questions.q: What does a streamed CDC event typically carry?
options: The operation type (insert/update/delete), the row's state before and after, and when the change happened
Only the table name, with no row-level detail
A full nightly snapshot of the entire table
Only the primary key, with no other fields
questions.explain: That's everything downstream needs to apply the exact same change somewhere else.

questions.q: How does streamed CDC differ from the batch MERGE INTO covered in Databricks & Delta Lake's Lesson 22?
options: CDC applies changes continuously as they happen; MERGE runs periodically and compares a batch of incoming rows against an existing table
They solve completely unrelated problems
MERGE INTO only works with streaming data, never batch
CDC can only run once per day, like a batch job
questions.explain: Both keep a downstream copy in sync with row-level changes, but on different rhythms — continuous vs. periodic.

questions.q: Why does CDC avoid adding extra query load to the source database, unlike repeatedly polling it for changes?
options: CDC reads the database's own internal change log, which it's already maintaining for its own purposes, rather than running extra queries against it
CDC doesn't actually read anything from the source database
Polling is always faster than CDC, so this isn't really an advantage
CDC only works on databases with no production traffic
questions.explain: There's no extra query load on the source at all, since the change log already exists for the database's own use.

questions.q: Is streamed CDC best suited for data that changes slowly and batch-friendly, or operational data needing near-real-time sync?
options: Operational data needing near-real-time sync — batch MERGE is the better fit for slowly-changing, batch-friendly data
Streamed CDC is only useful for data that never changes
Batch MERGE is always superior regardless of the data's change pattern
There's no meaningful difference in which scenario fits which approach
questions.explain: The choice depends on how the specific data actually behaves and how quickly downstream systems need to reflect its changes.
